t.1.43.1: The Sūta said: Then Vāsuki spoke these words to the seer Jaratkāru: "This maiden bears the same name as you; she is my sister, endowed with austerity."
t.1.43.2: I will support your wife; accept her, O best of the twice-born. And I will guard her with all my power, O ascetic rich in penance.
t.1.43.3: When the Nāga had promised, "I shall support my sister," Jaratkāru then went to the serpent's dwelling.
t.1.43.4: There the foremost of those who know the mantras, great in austerity and of mighty vows, the righteous-souled one, took her hand in marriage, honoring it with due rite and mantras.
t.1.43.6: A bed had been prepared there, covered with splendid spreads, and there Jaratkāru dwelt, with his wife as his companion.
t.1.43.5: Then, taking his wife and praised by the great seers, he went to the splendid chamber that the lord of serpents had approved.
t.1.43.7: There that best of the virtuous made a compact with his wife: "Nothing displeasing to me is ever to be done, nor ever to be said."
t.1.43.8: For if anything displeasing is done to me, I shall abandon you and my dwelling in your house. Accept this word which has been spoken by me.
t.1.43.9: Then she, the sister of the lord of the Nāgas, deeply agitated and filled with great sorrow, spoke these words to him: "So be it."
t.1.43.11: Then once, at the time of her season, having bathed, the sister of Vāsuki approached her husband, that great sage, in the proper manner.
t.1.43.10: In just the same way, that glorious woman, eager to please, served her husband of difficult temper with means as rare as a white crow.
t.1.43.12: There an embryo came into being within her, resembling blazing fire, exceedingly endowed with ascetic power, with a radiance equal to Vaiśvānara. Just as the moon waxes in the bright fortnight, even so did it grow.
t.1.43.13: Then, after some days, Jaratkāru of great austerity placed his head in her lap and fell asleep, as though utterly weary.
t.1.43.14: And while that foremost of brahmins slept, the sun was about to go down to the mountain of setting as the day drew to its close, O brahman; then the sister of Vāsuki, high-minded and fearful of a lapse in dharma, began to reflect.
t.1.43.15: Which would be the good deed for me, to wake my husband or not? For this righteous man is of a difficult temper; how may I avoid offending him?
t.1.43.16: On the one hand there is the anger of a man devoted to dharma, on the other the loss of dharma; "the loss of dharma would surely be the graver matter here," thus she made up her mind.
t.1.43.18: Having thus resolved in her mind, Jaratkāru, the serpent-woman, sweet of speech, then spoke these gentle words to that seer of blazing austerity, who lay there like a fire.
t.1.43.17: If I wake him, he will surely become angry; yet if the twilight rite is passed over, there will certainly be a loss of his dharma.
t.1.43.19: Rise, O greatly fortunate one, the sun is going to its setting. Touch water, O blessed one, and, firm in your vows, perform the twilight worship.
t.1.43.21: Thus addressed, the blessed Jaratkāru of great austerities, his lips trembling, spoke these words to his wife.
t.1.43.20: This hour, in which the agnihotra fires have been kindled, is at once lovely and dreadful; and twilight is now setting in in the western quarter, my lord.
t.1.43.22: O serpent-woman, you have shown me this insult; I will not dwell near you any longer, I shall go back the way I came.
t.1.43.23: Surely, O fair-thighed one, the sun has not the power to set at its proper time while I lie asleep; this is what dwells in my heart.
t.1.43.24: No one at all would wish to dwell here once he has been slighted; how much less, then, one devoted to dharma, such as I or one like me?
t.1.43.25: Thus told these heart-shaking words by her husband, Jaratkāru, the sister of Vāsuki, spoke there in Vāsuki's dwelling.
t.1.43.27: Thus addressed, the great ascetic seer Jaratkāru, filled with anger and wishing to abandon his serpent wife, spoke to his wife.
t.1.43.26: It was not out of disrespect that I awakened you. I did this so that there might be no lapse in your dharma, O brahmin.
t.1.43.30: Thus addressed, the flawless-limbed Jaratkāru, overwhelmed by anxiety and grief, then replied to her husband Jaratkāru.
t.1.43.28: My speech has never spoken an untruth; I shall go, O serpent lady. For this agreement was made by me with you, between us, long before.
t.1.43.29: I have dwelt here happily, good lady; when I have gone, lovely and timid one, you should tell your brother, 'He has gone away; that blessed one has departed.' And you too ought not to grieve when I have left.
t.1.43.31: Then the fair-hipped, lovely-thighed woman, her palms joined in reverence and her eyes brimming with tears, summoned her courage, with a voice choked by tears, a mouth gone dry, and a heart that trembled.
t.1.43.32: O knower of dharma, you who stand firm in dharma, you ought not to abandon me, a blameless woman who stands firm in dharma and always delights in what is dear and beneficial to you.
t.1.43.34: O best of the good, a child from you was desired for the sake of my kinsmen, who are overcome by their mother's curse, and that child is not yet to be seen.
t.1.43.33: And as for the purpose for which I was given to you, O best of the twice-born, what will Vāsuki say to me, a foolish woman who has not attained it?
t.1.43.35: For by obtaining offspring from you, welfare would come to my kinsmen; this union of mine with you should not be fruitless, O twice-born one.
t.1.43.37: Thus addressed, the sage Jaratkāru, rich in austerity, spoke to his wife words that were fitting and proper.
t.1.43.36: Desiring the welfare of my kinsmen, O blessed one, I seek to win your favour. O best of the virtuous, having placed in me this embryo whose form is not yet manifest, how can you, being great-souled, wish to go away, abandoning a blameless woman?
t.1.43.38: There is this embryo within you, O fortunate one, resembling Vaiśvānara, the fire; he will be a seer of supremely righteous soul, one who has mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
t.1.43.39: Having spoken thus, the righteous-souled great seer Jaratkāru, his resolve firmly made, went away once more to fierce austerity.
